title: Psychedelics, entactogens and psychoplastogens for depression and related disorders - Hoyer - British Journal of Pharmacology - Wiley Online Library

Currently, the most actively investigated rapidly acting antidepressants, anxiolytics and/or anti PTSD agents, include psychedelics e.g. psilocybin, LSD, N,N-dimethyltryptamine, ayahuasca; non-hallucinogenic entactogens, e.g. MDMA; psychoplastogens which rapidly promote neuroplasticity, e.g. ibogaine, ketamine and esketamine; and other atypicals e.g. dextromorphan/bupropion, esmethadone. Late-stage clinical trials support psychedelics and/or MDMA-assisted psychotherapy as rapidly acting treatments for major depressive disorder (MDD), treatment-resistant depression (TRD), PTSD or generalised anxiety disorders (GAD).
Together, these findings strongly support a biological basis for MDD, GAD, PTSD and related conditions, which can be considered as mixed biochemical, neurological and neuroimmune disorders, and are profoundly modified by psychedelics, entactogens and the newly developed psychoplastogens. The resurgence of interest in a diversity of psychedelics and related compounds for the treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD) and related disorders has prompted a further examination of the role of 5-HT (serotonin) in such conditions, alongside other mechanisms of drug action.
More recently, Guy Goodwin and colleagues (Goodwin et al., 2024a, 2024b; O'Donnell et al., 2024; Pasculli et al., 2024) have been arguing that the current clinical trials with psilocybin in depression should not be defined as psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy (as is the case for MDMA in PTSD), because psychiatrists/psychologists are only present during the active treatment for safety reasons, not for psychotherapy sessions. Obviously, treatment with psychoplastogens lacking psychedelic effects, will not require assisted psychotherapy (Dong et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2021; Ly et al., 2021; Peters & Olson, 2021; Vargas et al., 2021).
Depression may be described as a long lasting network dysfunction which can be treated by psychoplastogens; various other neuropsychiatric diseases show decreased cortical dendritic spine density as well. The ability to promote cortical neuron growth has been suggested as the mechanism underlying the rapid and sustained therapeutic effects of psychedelics, entactogens and other antidepressants that affect the BDNF/TrkB/mTORC1 system (Aguilar-Valles et al., 2021; Cameron, Patel, et al., 2023; De Martin et al., 2021; Fogaça et al., 2019; Hutten et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023; Moliner et al., 2023).
